items.example_en: Hello, my name is Mary.
items.note: Two third tones in a row: the first becomes a rising tone, so it sounds like ní hǎo.

items.example_en: Hello, who are you looking for?
items.note: 您 is the respectful you, for elders, customers, and officials.

items.example_en: Good morning, have you eaten?
items.note: Among friends, just 早 works.

items.example_en: Long time no see, how are you?
items.note: Textbook Chinese. Natives more often ask 最近怎么样？

items.example_en: Hello, what is your name?
items.note: Question words stay where the answer goes; no word order change.

items.example: 很高兴认识你，我是保罗。
items.example_en: Nice to meet you, I'm Paul.
items.note: Literally very happy to know you.

items.example_en: Please give me a coffee.
items.note: Goes at the start of the request, not the end.

items.example_en: Thank you for your help.
items.note: The second syllable is unstressed and toneless.

items.example_en: Thanks! You're welcome.
items.note: 不 changes from bù to bú before a fourth tone.

items.example_en: Sorry, I'm late.
items.note: A real apology, heavier than 不好意思.

items.example: 不好意思，请问洗手间在哪儿？
items.example_en: Excuse me, where is the toilet?
items.note: The everyday way to get attention or apologise for a small thing.

items.example_en: Sorry for the trouble, thank you.
items.note: Said after someone has done you a favour.

items.example_en: Goodbye, see you tomorrow!
items.note: Literally again see. 明天见 is see you tomorrow.

items.example_en: OK, bye bye!
items.note: Borrowed from English, very common in speech and messages.

items.example_en: Sorry, I don't understand.
items.note: A potential complement: 听得懂 means able to understand by listening.

items.english: please speak a bit more slowly
items.example_en: Please speak a bit more slowly, thank you.
items.note: 一点 after an adjective means a bit more of it.

items.english: how do you say this in Chinese?
items.example_en: How do you say this in Chinese?
items.note: 用 plus a language means using that language.

items.pronunciation: wǒ de Zhōngwén bú tài hǎo
items.example: 不好意思，我的中文不太好。
items.example_en: Sorry, my Chinese isn't very good.
items.note: 不太 softens a negative: not very, rather than not at all.

items.example_en: My name is Stijn, and you?
items.note: Literally I am called. 我姓 gives the surname only.

items.example: 我是比利时人，但住在法国。
items.example_en: I'm Belgian, but I live in France.
items.note: Country plus 人 makes the nationality. No article, no plural.

items.example_en: I come from Ghent.
items.note: 从 marks the origin and goes before the verb, unlike English.

items.example_en: I've been living in Beijing for three years.
items.note: 了 at the end signals a state continuing up to now.

items.example: 我三十岁，我弟弟二十八岁。
items.example_en: I'm thirty, my younger brother is twenty-eight.
items.note: No verb at all with ages: subject plus number plus 岁.

items.example: 我有一个姐姐和一个弟弟。
items.example_en: I have an older sister and a younger brother.
items.note: Chinese distinguishes older and younger siblings lexically.

items.example_en: I work at a school.
items.note: 在 plus place comes before the verb: the place frames the action.

items.example_en: I'm a student, I study biology.
items.note: No article. 是 is required with a noun, unlike with adjectives.

items.example_en: And you, what do you do?
items.note: The natural way to ask about someone's job.

items.example: 我在学中文，学了六个月了。
items.example_en: I'm learning Chinese, I've been at it six months.
items.note: 在 before a verb marks an action in progress.

items.example_en: I can speak a little bit of Chinese.
items.note: 会 expresses a learned ability, unlike 能 or 可以.

items.example: 不好意思，你会说英文吗？
items.example_en: Excuse me, can you speak English?
items.note: 吗 turns any statement into a yes-no question.

items.example_en: Three coffees, thank you.
items.note: 二 counts, 两 is used before a measure word: 两杯, not 二杯.

items.example_en: Ten yuan in total.
items.note: Numbers 11 to 19 are 十一, 十二 and so on: perfectly regular.

items.example: 公交车二十分钟以后到。
items.example_en: The bus arrives in twenty minutes.
items.note: Literally two tens. The whole system is built this way.

items.example_en: This ticket is a hundred yuan.
items.note: 一 shifts tone before other tones: yìbǎi, yí ge.

items.example_en: This computer costs over ten thousand.
items.note: Chinese groups by ten thousands, not thousands. 十万 is a hundred thousand.

items.example_en: How much is this bag?
items.note: 多少 for open quantities, 几 when the answer is under about ten.

items.example_en: Excuse me, what time is it?
items.note: 几 expects a small number, which clock hours always are.

items.example_en: It's a quarter past eight.
items.note: 点 is the measure word for the hour.

items.example_en: The train leaves at half past eight.
items.note: 半 is half. 一刻 is a quarter, 差一刻 is a quarter to.

items.example_en: I run in the park in the morning.
items.note: The time expression comes before the verb, never after.

items.example_en: The weather is nice today.
items.note: 昨天 yesterday, 明天 tomorrow. All built on 天.

items.example: 我下班以后给你打电话。
items.example_en: I'll call you after work.
items.note: Comes AFTER the clause it applies to, the mirror image of English.

items.example_en: See you on Monday.
items.note: Literally week one. Sunday is 星期天 or 星期日.

items.example_en: What are you doing this weekend?
My birthday is in January.
items.note: Months are simply number plus 月: 一月, 二月, 十二月.

items.example_en: Let's discuss it again next week.
items.note: 下 is next, 上 is last: 上个星期 was last week.

items.example_en: The shops are closed on the first of May.
items.note: Big to small: year, month, day. 号 in speech, 日 in writing.

items.example_en: I always have breakfast at home.
items.note: Adverbs go before the verb: 总是吃, never 吃总是.
